summary: Describes an architecture for sending IP datagrams over MPEG-2 Transport Streams, which are used for digital TV and also as a subnetwork technology. It identifies the need for Internet standards for the interface between the stream and an IP network. It suggests a new encapsulation method and protocols for address resolution and association with logical channels.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4259 describes how IP datagrams could be carried over MPEG-2 Transport Streams used for digital television and data networks. It outlines packet wrapping and address-resolution requirements but does not define the protocols that meet them.

what is a pid in mpeg-2
what is address resolution over mpeg-2
subtitle: An architecture and requirements for carrying IP datagrams over MPEG-2 transport streams.

tldr.problem: MPEG-2 Transport Streams carry digital television and can serve as subnetworks, but existing encapsulation methods were not designed to provide an efficient, flexible IP interface.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes transport-stream channels identified by PIDs, requirements for encapsulating IP packets, and address-resolution functions that map IP destinations to a multiplex, PID, and receiver address.
tldr.outcome: This is an architecture and requirements document, not an encapsulation or address-resolution protocol. It identifies ULE and an address-resolution protocol as separate work in progress at the time.

today: RFC 4259 is an Informational RFC published in November 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its references describe ULE and an address-resolution protocol as work in progress at that time.

sections.title: IP Services over MPEG-2
sections.content:
MPEG-2 Transport Streams (TS) are used for digital television and as a subnetwork technology. RFC 4259 describes an architecture for carrying IP datagrams over these streams, including systems based on Digital Video Broadcast and ATSC standards.

Many such networks are unidirectional and have limited bandwidth. The RFC says an IP encapsulation should add little overhead, require modest processing, handle errors, and allow later extension.
sections.plainLanguage: MPEG-2 streams can carry IP traffic as well as television data. This RFC describes the network components and requirements needed to support that use.

sections.title: Transport Streams and Logical Channels
sections.content:
An MPEG-2 multiplex contains parallel Transport Stream Logical Channels. Each channel is identified by a Packet Identifier (PID) carried in the header of each TS Packet. A TS Packet is 188 bytes long and has a 4-byte header; the PID is 13 bits wide.

An Encapsulator turns a packet such as an IP datagram into a Sub-Network Data Unit (SNDU), then fragments it across TS Packets. A Receiver selects the PIDs it needs and reassembles each SNDU. Re-multiplexors may change PID values, so PIDs are not end-to-end identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The stream has numbered logical channels. An encapsulator wraps an IP packet and sends it in pieces; a receiver selects the right channel and rebuilds the packet.

sections.title: Requirements for Encapsulating IP
sections.content:
The RFC describes existing approaches, including ATM AAL5 and Multi-Protocol Encapsulation (MPE), and explains why an IP-centric encapsulation could be useful. Its requirements include support for IPv4 and IPv6, a protocol-type field, an optional Network Point of Attachment (NPA) address, and extension headers.

The encapsulation needs to mark where payload units begin and identify their length, so a receiver can distinguish one SNDU from another and reassemble fragments. It also needs an integrity check in a trailer. The RFC says a CRC-32 is sufficient for a payload up to 12 KB.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet wrapper needs to identify what it carries, where it ends, and whether it was damaged. It should support IPv4, IPv6, optional receiver addresses, and future extensions.

sections.title: Address Resolution for Unicast and Multicast
sections.content:
Address resolution links an IP address to link-layer information. In MPEG-2, a sender or receiver may need a receiver identifier, a PID or a way to find one, and tuning information such as a transmission frequency. Re-multiplexors may change PIDs, which makes an indirect lookup useful.

The RFC considers information carried in MPEG-2 signaling tables, tables carried over IP, or an IP query-and-response protocol. It calls for scoping so private or local addresses do not leak into other addressed areas, and for authentication of address-resolution information. Multicast support must map IP groups to a PID and multiplex and let receivers locate the matching flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Address resolution tells a sender which stream and channel can reach a receiver. The information must be scoped to the right network and authenticated when needed.

sections.title: Security and Link Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC recommends end-to-end security for communication paths, especially those using wireless or broadcast links. It also notes that subnetwork protection can help protect control functions such as address resolution.

Encrypting a whole Transport Stream can also encrypt the receiver address, requiring a receiver to decrypt packets before filtering them, and may require receivers to share a key. The RFC recommends that a new encapsulation allow Transport Stream encryption and optional link-level encryption or authentication. It makes no IANA requests itself.
sections.plainLanguage: End-to-end protection remains important, especially on broadcast links. Link encryption can add protection too, but encrypting receiver addresses affects how receivers filter packets.
